pack.title: Trim: an old land, a grant and a castle at the ford

presentation.era: twelfth to early thirteenth century, with a present-town afterlife
presentation.anchor: Hugh de Lacy · 1172 grant · Áth Troim · Trim Castle and town
presentation.question: What does a royal document claim to give, and how does a ford become a contested castle centre?
presentation.opening: Six chapters begin with existing Meath, read the grant as a claim, move to Trim's ford, follow the first timber fortification through attack, inspect the stone castle's phases, and return the monument to a living town.
presentation.evidenceLimit: The pack uses later grant copies, the Song of Dermot, topography, official site interpretation and surviving fabric. It does not equate grant with consent, invent a foundation day, assign every wall without review or speak for everyone affected by conquest.

presentation.sourceDetail: Claims M01–M05 and M07 · grant-copy citation, castle phasing and conquest-sensitivity review remain open
presentation.artifactPrompt: Carry the copied grant, ford map, timber sequence, stone phases and conquest boundary together.
presentation.tegCanDo: Recognise and produce supported Irish for possession, place, building, residence and description inside a conquest-sensitive site account.

chapters.title: An Talamh roimh an Deontas · The land before the grant

pages.title: A grant does not begin the land
pages.body: The talamh that Henry II would grant already held an old kingdom, churches, routes, settlements and political claims. Sean means old; baile means town or settlement; ainm means name. Those words come first so the story cannot present Meath as blank space awaiting a castle.
pages.detail: The county opens with existing place and authority before the new documentary claim arrives.
pages.visualCaption: Generated editorial interpretation of the Boyne ford landscape · not documentary evidence

pages.title: Mide was a political country, not a future estate
pages.body: Medieval Mide extended beyond the boundaries of the modern county. Its rulers, churches and communities had their own histories and rivalries. The later lordship reused a famous territorial name while changing who claimed authority over it.
pages.detail: Modern county, earlier kingdom and Anglo-Norman lordship overlap; they are not identical shapes.

displayItems.title: Lordship of Meath
displayItems.detail: A later grant and conquest claim

pages.title: Place-names carry older ground
pages.body: Áth Troim will matter later as the ford chosen for the new lordship's centre. Naming it now establishes continuity: the castle takes position at an already named crossing. A new fortification does not create the river, ford or memory of the place.
pages.detail: The name is evidence of place continuity, not proof that every later story about its origin is exact.

pages.title: No surviving account speaks for everyone in Meath
pages.body: Royal documents, conquest narratives, annals, archaeology and later built fabric preserve different interests. None is the neutral voice of the land. The story will let a grant make its claim while refusing to make that claim the same thing as consent.
pages.detail: The conquest-sensitivity rule begins before the conquering document enters the screen.

pages.title: The opening corrects a frame; it does not recreate a court
pages.body: The account can establish that Meath was an inhabited political territory and that Trim was an existing named place. It cannot reconstruct one representative Gaelic household as if that family could stand for every person affected by conquest.
pages.detail: The learner remains an observer of evidence rather than a fictional resident assigned one voice.

pages.title: A document is about to claim what already exists
pages.body: The old land, settlement and name remain in view as a new paper claim arrives. In 1172 Henry II grants Meath to Hugh de Lacy. The next chapter reads what possession language can reveal—and what it can conceal.
pages.detail: The change is a new claim to authority over existing land.

chapters.title: Éileamh ar Pháipéar · A claim on paper

pages.title: A king says the land is Hugh's
pages.body: Henry II granted the talamh of Meath to Hugh de Lacy. The old baile and ainm remain beneath that sentence. Irish expresses possession through agam and agat—at me, at you—rather than a direct verb meaning have. That grammar makes the chapter's question unusually sharp: what does a document say someone has?
pages.detail: The language focus exposes possession as a relationship and claim, not a neutral fact.

pages.title: The grant survives through later copies
pages.body: The 1172 grant is known through later manuscript copies and antiquarian transmission rather than one pristine charter in front of the learner. Final production needs a pinned copy, transcription and modern paraphrase before showing document text.
pages.detail: The app can state the grant at chapter level while keeping the exact wording behind a historian gate.

pages.title: New words do not make a new world
pages.context: nua · new · tóg · take or raise
pages.body: Nua means new. Tóg can mean take, lift or raise and will later carry castle building. Here the document offers a new claim to old land. Hugh still had to turn paper authority into control through alliances, delegation, fortification and violence.
pages.detail: The grant is a consequential act, but it is not self-executing possession.

pages.title: Hear the possession question
pages.context: Tá taifead nua agam; cad atá agat? Tóg é
pages.body: Listen to agam, agat, nua and tóg in one exchange.

exercise.objective: Hear the possession forms and new-record action in context.
exercise.prompt: Listen, then build the full exchange.
exercise.answer: Tá taifead nua agam; cad atá agat? Tóg é.
exercise.translation: I have a new record; what do you have? Take it.
exercise.audioText: Tá taifead nua agam; cad atá agat? Tóg é.
exercise.modelText: Tá taifead nua agam; cad atá agat? Tóg é.
exercise.feedback: The line asks who has the new record before instructing the learner to take it.
exercise.hint: Build Tá taifead nua agam first; cad atá agat follows.
exercise.recovery: Keep tóg é together as the final instruction.

pages.title: A royal grant is not local consent
pages.body: The charter records what Henry claimed power to give and what Hugh was expected to hold. It does not record agreement from the people, churches or rulers whose land and obligations were being reassigned.
pages.detail: This sentence is the conquest-sensitivity hinge and must survive Learning-mode abridgement.

pages.title: What the grant does not list
pages.body: The copied grant centres king, grantee, territory and service. It does not inventory every community, church, right or dependency affected by the transfer. That silence is structural: a document made to confer lordship is not a census of those placed beneath it.
pages.detail: The learner should notice who is named, who is grouped into land and what kinds of relationship disappear from the document.

pages.title: The document proves a grant, not possession on the ground
pages.body: The grant is strong evidence that Henry conferred Meath on Hugh in 1172. Its words alone cannot prove the reach of immediate control, identify every displaced claim or turn resistance into a footnote.
pages.detail: Paper and ground remain separate evidence registers throughout the county.

pages.title: A paper centre needs a physical centre
pages.body: To hold a vast lordship, Hugh needed places from which authority could be organised and defended. Trim's ford and river offered one such centre. The next chapter leaves the copied grant and reads the ground.
pages.detail: The story shifts from documentary claim to topographic choice.

chapters.title: Áth Troim · The ford of Trim

pages.title: The ford makes Trim useful
pages.body: The possession question from the grant remains open: Cad atá agat? The claim is nua — new — but paper does not control the ground. To tóg — raise — a centre, Hugh turns to place. An áth is a ford and an abhainn is a river; anseo and ansiúd make the site readable.
pages.detail: Topography explains why the lordship's centre forms here without implying that strategic value equals consent.
pages.visualCaption: Generated editorial interpretation of water moving through the Boyne ford · not documentary evidence

displayItems.title: anseo · ansiúd
displayItems.detail: Here and there across the site

pages.title: Trim becomes the lordship's centre
pages.body: Trim served as the caput, the chief centre, of the lordship. The ford, river and surrounding routes gave physical form to a grant whose territory was much larger than any one castle could see.
pages.detail: Caput is introduced as a historical term, not as a claim that all Meath became orderly from this point.
pages.advanceLabel: Place the centre in the wider land

pages.title: The crossing remains in the name
pages.body: The place-name keeps the áth visible even when later visitors first notice towers and walls. The river is not scenery behind the castle. It is part of the reason the centre was chosen and part of the older place the fortification occupied.
pages.detail: Language returns attention from monument to site.
pages.advanceLabel: Read the ford in the name

pages.title: A strategic place is still a contested place
pages.body: The ford helps explain why Hugh chose Trim as a centre. It does not make the seizure of authority inevitable, peaceful or beneficial to everyone already tied to the land. Route logic answers where, not whether the conquest was accepted.
pages.detail: The distinction must survive every map and diagram.

pages.title: The ground explains selection, not intention
pages.body: The Boyne crossing, surviving castle and historical consensus support Trim as the lordship's centre. They do not preserve Hugh's private first impression of the site or a single recorded moment of choice.
pages.detail: A map can show conditions and relationships without staging an arrival scene.

pages.title: The chosen centre needs enclosure
pages.context: Chapter turn · ford to first fortification
pages.body: Once the grant and crossing are joined, the next action is physical. A house, trench and stockade appear in the conquest narrative; defenders, attackers and rebuilding turn the claimed centre into a contested one.
pages.detail: The story moves from site logic to the first recorded fortification and its destruction.

chapters.title: An Chéad Daingean · The first fortification

pages.title: The first castle is a fortified house
pages.body: The áth and abhainn return anseo; the wider baile remains ansiúd. The Song of Dermot describes Hugh de Lacy fortifying a teach at Trim, cutting a trench and enclosing it with a stockade. That first caisleán was timber and earth, not the great stone keep visible today.
pages.detail: Teach and caisleán enter together so the learner can distinguish inhabited building from later monumental image.

pages.title: The enclosure is attacked and abandoned
pages.body: The poem describes Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair's forces moving against Trim. Hugh Tyrrel's defenders abandon the position; the attackers throw down the fortification; the site is later refortified. The sequence preserves resistance, not a smooth march of construction.
pages.detail: The conquest source has its own loyalties and rhetoric. Its sequence is valuable without adopting every judgement in its voice.

pages.title: People live inside what maps call a strongpoint
pages.body: Cónaí names living or residence; seas means stand. A fortification required people to keep watch, repair timber, store supplies and occupy a vulnerable position. The evidence does not name their private routines, but it does not permit the castle to become an empty military symbol.
pages.detail: The learner attends to human occupation without inventing a household guide.

pages.title: The poem calls some people noble and others rebels
pages.body: The Song's labels reveal the perspective of an Anglo-Norman conquest narrative. The app uses its details about house, trench, stockade, attack and rebuilding while refusing to repeat partisan labels as neutral description.
pages.detail: Source voice becomes inspectable evidence, not invisible narration.

pages.title: A conquest poem preserves action through rhetoric
pages.body: The poem supports an early fortified house, trench, stockade, attack and rebuilding. Archaeology and later fabric help place that sequence. Exact troop numbers, speeches and moral labels require separate scrutiny.
pages.detail: The chapter keeps the valuable event sequence and marks the source's partisan frame.

pages.title: Timber gives way to a longer stone project
pages.context: Chapter turn · early fort to keep
pages.body: The first enclosure can be built, broken and rebuilt quickly. The stone castle that dominates Trim belongs to a longer sequence under Hugh, Walter and their successors. The next chapter reads its walls as phases rather than one foundation day.
pages.detail: The story changes scale and material while keeping the earlier contested ground visible.

chapters.title: Caisleán Cloiche · The stone castle
chapters.place: Trim · late twelfth and early thirteenth century

pages.title: Stone makes the claim monumental
pages.context: Trim Castle · late twelfth and early thirteenth century
pages.body: The earlier teach, caisleán, cónaí and instruction seas return in cloch. A mór keep, defensive balla, ditch and moat turn the centre into a vast built statement. Féach means look: inspect joints, openings and changes rather than read the whole castle as one moment.
pages.detail: The later stone monument is a sequence of work, not the first fortification enlarged in a single uninterrupted campaign.
pages.visualCaption: Generated editorial interpretation of light moving across Trim's curtain wall · not documentary evidence

pages.title: The castle takes decades, not a day
pages.body: Heritage Ireland describes Hugh de Lacy and his successors taking about thirty years to build the castle. The great keep changed through phases; later walls, gates and domestic buildings added further layers.
pages.detail: A date range and named succession are more honest than a single ceremonial foundation scene.

pages.title: The keep resists a simple front
pages.body: The central keep is cruciform and presents twenty exterior faces. Its shape creates projecting angles, internal rooms and changing views as the learner moves around it. The plan is evidence of design and adaptation, not merely a dramatic silhouette.
pages.detail: A measured diagram can carry more truth than an uncleared cinematic reconstruction.

displayItems.detail: Use and defence inside the mass

pages.title: The keep is residence and coercive architecture
pages.body: Rooms, chapel, storage and circulation show a place used by elite households and administration. Ditch, wall, gate and height show defence and control. Calling it only a home softens its political work; calling it only a weapon erases the lives organised within it.
pages.detail: The story holds domestic and coercive functions together.

pages.title: Later use changes the stronghold
pages.body: The keep was altered as the de Lacy lordship and later occupation changed. Additional levels and adapted rooms show that even the most commanding form was not fixed at first completion.
pages.detail: The exact attribution of each alteration remains part of the castle-specialist gate; the secure learner claim is continued change.

pages.title: The present walls do not share one date
pages.body: The fabric supports a long building history under Hugh, Walter and later lords. Exact attribution of every wall, floor and opening requires castle-specialist review. The draft keeps broad phases but does not colour-code individual stones as settled fact.
pages.detail: The phasing gate must close before final diagrams or learner questions claim exact builders.

pages.title: The castle becomes part of a town
pages.context: Chapter turn · monument to lived place
pages.body: Stone makes the lordship's centre durable and visually dominant, but Trim does not end at the curtain wall. Streets, worship, work, households and later memories gather around it. The final chapter returns the monument to the town and the conquest to its afterlife.
pages.detail: The story widens from fabric to a lived and contested place.

pages.title: The wall stands inside a living town
pages.body: The mór balla and cloch of the caisleán remain, but Trim is also a baile where people have cónaí now. Féach returns as an instruction to look beyond the keep: river, ford, streets, later buildings and older names continue around it.
pages.detail: The closing chapter refuses to let monumental conquest architecture become the whole county.

displayItems.title: Town
displayItems.detail: A lived place beyond the wall

pages.title: Urban life grows beside lordship
pages.body: A town developed beside the castle, with its own streets, worship, trade and later defences. Its history cannot be reduced to service of the keep. People negotiated, benefited from, endured and resisted changing systems of power in different ways.
pages.detail: The town is not a decorative epilogue; it is the human afterlife of the chosen centre.

pages.title: Old fabric and new life occupy one place
pages.body: The castle is sean; the town is not frozen around it. Nua returns through present use, conservation and changing streets. The name Áth Troim still carries the ford even when the crossing is no longer the visitor's first thought.
pages.detail: Afterlife means continuity and change, not nostalgic stillness.

options.text: Bhí sé nua; tá sé sean anois.
Bhí sé sean; tá sé nua anois.
Tá sé nua agus sean.

exercise.hint: Bhí places the first state in the past; tá brings the second to now.
exercise.recovery: Choose the line with nua first and sean anois second.

pages.title: Built beauty does not erase dispossession
pages.body: Trim Castle is architecturally remarkable and historically coercive. Admiring its design does not require celebrating conquest as progress. The county account keeps the grant, attack, control and older Meath visible beside the surviving monument.
pages.detail: Multiple truths can share one screen when their relationship is stated plainly.

pages.title: What this county account can claim
pages.context: Land · grant · ford · fort · castle · town
pages.body: The account can establish an existing Meath, a 1172 grant, Trim's strategic ford, an early fortified house attacked and rebuilt, a stone castle developed in phases, and a town growing beside it. It cannot turn a later grant copy into consent, assign every wall exactly or speak for everyone dispossessed.
pages.detail: The final evidence page gathers the county's causal chain and open specialist limits.

pages.title: Carry the crossing beneath the castle
pages.body: Meath closes with the ford still legible beneath the monumental keep and the old land still legible beneath the grant. The castle enters What survives; any learner site diagram enters What you made; the twenty words enter review only after Learning completion.
pages.detail: Story completion can advance the route without turning the county gold.
